What 100,000 orders actually say about delivery

Six analyses on the Olist Brazilian marketplace, run against a tested Kimball star schema rather than raw files. The headline is uncomfortable for the usual narrative: most lateness is not the seller's fault, and the part that is is small, cheap to instrument, and shockingly predictive.

Every number below comes from the built marts, not from spreadsheets. The project moves the raw nine-table export through staging, intermediate and mart layers; the facts are at two grains (order and order line), dimensions are surrogate-keyed, and referential integrity is enforced by relationships tests. The analyses then ask questions the business would actually ask, and are explicit about what the data cannot support.

Insight 01 · Customer experience

Missing the promised date costs about two and a half stars

The delivery estimate is a promise, and the review score tracks whether it was kept far more closely than it tracks how fast the parcel was.

Finding

Early deliveries average 4.29 stars and on-time deliveries 4.04. Slip by a few days and the average falls to 2.99; slip by a week or more and it sits at 1.74. The same drop survives controls for product category, weight band and distance — lateness is roughly twenty times the effect of distance alone.

Evidence

  • Late orders are only 6.8% of delivered volume but dominate the 1- and 2-star tail that drags the platform rating.
  • The cliff is at the boundary, not in the middle: the biggest single step is from on time to 1–5 days late.
  • Arriving early scores higher than arriving exactly on time, which is why the recommendation is to keep estimates conservative rather than optimistic.
Recommendation

Optimise for hitting the promised date, not raw speed. Most orders already arrive early; the leverage is the small share that misses, especially long-haul ones where a realistic estimate and a proactive delay notice are cheaper than expediting.

Insight 02 · Operations

Lateness is geography, not product or seller quality

If you had to pick one variable to explain a late delivery, it is the distance between the customer and the seller — and that is a network-design question, not a coaching one.

Evidence

  • Late rate more than doubles from 4.5% under 100km to 10.5% beyond 1000km.
  • Product category is negligible: 6.3% to 8.0% across all categories with enough volume.
  • Weight matters only in the 10kg+ tail; below that it is flat.
  • Sellers are spread, not concentrated: of 881 sellers with 20+ delivered items, only 11 are chronically late.
  • Two event spikes stand out — 12.4% in November 2017 (Black Friday) and 19.0% in March 2018, which insight 06 resolves.
Recommendation

Shorten routes by fulfilling from the nearest seller, pre-scale capacity around known peaks, and widen estimates on long lanes. Coach the mid-tail; do not mass-cull, because the always-late group is too small to explain the aggregate.

Insight 03 · Revenue risk

Revenue concentrates on sellers, not categories

The classic marketplace worry is category dependence. Here the risk is supply-side and personal: a few hundred sellers carry two thirds of everything sold.

Evidence

  • Top 10% of sellers: 67.6% of GMV. Top 20%: 82.7%. Bottom half: about 2% combined.
  • No single category exceeds 9.3% of revenue; the top five are about 40%, and it takes roughly 20 of 72 categories to reach 80%.
  • Seller quality does not vary with seller size, so there is no data reason to cap larger sellers.
Recommendation

Treat the top few hundred sellers as key accounts: retention there protects two thirds of revenue. Category strategy can stay broad, because no category is load-bearing on its own.

Insight 04 · Customer value

Value is concentrated, but the base is one-time buyers

RFM works as a value-tiering device and fails as a retention funnel. About 97% of customers order exactly once, so frequency carries almost no signal.

Evidence

  • Champions: 16.4% of customers, 30.2% of revenue.
  • At Risk: 15.5% of customers, 29.2% of revenue.
  • Frequency is tiered with CASE (1 / 3 / 5) rather than NTILE, because quintiles on a 97%-single-order distribution are meaningless.
Recommendation

Use the segments to prioritise spend, not to forecast churn. The At-Risk revenue figure is mostly one-time buyers who will never return, so a win-back budget should be sized against the small repeat cohort, not the segment total.

Insight 05 · Data quality

Payment mismatches are mechanics, not ingestion errors

A reconciliation test compares every order's payment total against item price plus freight. It fails on 387 orders, and the right engineering response was to explain them rather than fix them.

Evidence

  • 294 orders overpaid by an average of +R$10.44, consistent with installment interest.
  • 93 orders underpaid by an average of −R$2.15, consistent with vouchers and promotional discounts.
  • The test runs at WARN severity on purpose: a build that fails on legitimate payment mechanics trains people to ignore the build.
Insight 06 · New analysis

Only a quarter of lateness is the seller's fault

This is the analysis that reframes the others. Splitting each late order into "handed over after the seller's own deadline" versus "handed over on time and lost in transit" shows where the controllable leverage really is.

Finding

8,563 of 96,469 delivered orders (8.9%) are handed to the carrier after the seller's deadline. The median overshoot is one day and the 90th percentile is 7.8 days, so most are small slips — but the effect is brutal: an order shipped 7+ days late arrives late 59.8% of the time, against 5.4% for one shipped on time.

4,729 late orders (72.4%) were handed over on time. Only 1,804 (27.6%) trace back to a late handover. Even an overdue order still arrives on time 78.9% of the time, so a late handover is a strong signal of risk rather than a guarantee of failure. A seller-coaching programme addresses about a quarter of the problem — and that is the ceiling, not the midpoint.

Where it sits

  • Overdue share is flat across distance (9.5% under 100km, 9.2% beyond 1000km), so distance is not a seller-discipline story.
  • Among on-time handovers, the late rate climbs from 2.4% to 8.2% — that is the transit effect.
  • Sellers: of 804 with 20+ delivered orders, 75 sit above 25% overdue (6,812 orders) and 232 above 10%. Small, nameable tail.
  • States: overdue stays between 6.7% and 10.1% everywhere, while late delivery runs from 4.0% (PR) to 17.4% (MA).
  • March 2018 is the clean test: 8.4% overdue (normal) but 19.0% late. That spike is pure transit.

Recommendation

Instrument handover separately from transit. Alert the same day an order breaches its shipping deadline, coach the 75 named sellers, and treat the MA/CE/BA long-haul lanes as a carrier problem with its own SLA. The new delivery_risk mart (month × state × distance band) exists to serve exactly that view in the dashboard.

Method and grain

Population. Insight 06 uses delivered orders that have both a carrier handover timestamp and a delivery estimate (n = 96,469); cancellations and in-flight orders are excluded, as are orders with no line items. The shipping deadline is the latest item deadline for the order, and overdue hours run from that deadline to order_delivered_carrier_timestamp. Late means delivery_vs_estimate_days > 0.

Distance. Great-circle distance between deduplicated zip-prefix centroids, computed once in fct_order_items. It is null where a zip is missing, so distance cuts drop roughly 476 orders.

Grain. Insights 01–03 read order-grain or line-item-grain facts as appropriate; 04 and 05 read purpose-built marts. Multi-item orders are counted per order in insight 06 and per item in insight 02, which is why the 1000km+ late rate reads 10.5% here and 10.3% in the line-item analysis.

What this data cannot support. There is no cost of goods, so every revenue figure is gross merchandise value, not margin. customer_id is per-order, so all person-level analysis uses customer_unique_id. And with a ~3% repeat rate, RFM is descriptive segmentation rather than a retention model.
